name: 2018 Farm Bill
short: The Agriculture Improvement Act of 2018, which legalised hemp by defining it as cannabis with no more than 0.3% delta-9 THC and removing it from federal drug control.
definition: The 2018 Farm Bill, formally the Agriculture Improvement Act of 2018 (Public Law 115-334), is the law that made hemp a legal agricultural commodity in the US. Section 10113 defined hemp as Cannabis sativa L. and any part of the plant, including derivatives, extracts and cannabinoids, with a delta-9 THC concentration of no more than 0.3% on a dry-weight basis. It also removed hemp from the Controlled Substances Act's definition of marijuana. The 2014 Farm Bill had allowed hemp only in research pilot programs.

The law set up a USDA-supervised system of state, tribal and federal hemp production plans and left the FDA in charge of hemp-derived food, supplements and drugs. Its wording, which covered derivatives and named only delta-9 THC, opened the door to a multibillion-dollar market for intoxicating hemp products, including delta-8 THC, THCA flower and hemp-derived delta-9 edibles, often sold with little regulation.

Congress closed that path in November 2025 through a funding law, Public Law 119-37, which rewrote the hemp definition around total THC and a 0.4 mg per-container cap. Most of the change takes effect on 11 December 2026; the exclusion for cannabinoids the plant cannot naturally produce applies from 12 November 2026.
example: The delta-8 market grew out of a gap in the 2018 Farm Bill that Congress is now closing.
